The disciples' question is answered with a portrait of how the church lives between the two comings: deception, conflict, suffering, witness and the need for watchfulness are permanent features of the age. AD 70 is one striking embodiment of God's judgment on unfaithfulness, but the pattern repeats until Christ returns. The point of the answer is not a calendar but readiness.

The spiritual reading takes the disciples' admiration of stones as the starting point: Jesus is moving them from a religion centred on a building to himself as the true temple (John 2:19–21). The end of the age is the end of the old order of law and sacrifice, fulfilled at the cross and made visible in AD 70, and the “coming” is also understood as Christ's coming in power to his people and his presence within them. The discourse then becomes a call to discern false christs and remain anchored in the finished work of Christ.
Not one stone upon another

As Jesus leaves the temple, his disciples point out its buildings. He answers that every stone will be thrown down. The saying follows immediately after his lament over Jerusalem, “your house is left to you desolate” (23:38).

Herod's temple was among the wonders of the Roman east; the rabbis later said that whoever had not seen it had never seen a beautiful building. The disciples' remark is the natural pride of Galilean pilgrims. Jesus' prediction stands in the line of Micah 3:12 and Jeremiah 26:18, which foretold the ruin of the first temple, and in Matthew it is the climax of chapters 21–23, where he enters the temple, curses a fig tree, tells parables of rejected sons and tenants, and pronounces seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees.

The prophecy was literally fulfilled in AD 70, when Titus ordered the city and temple razed so that, in Josephus' words, nothing was left to make visitors believe it had ever been inhabited. The link with 23:36–38 is decisive: judgment on “this generation” and the desolation of “your house” set the subject of the whole discourse.

Full preterists agree that the temple's destruction is the subject, and add that, as the disciples' question shows, it is inseparable from the coming and the end of the age. The fall of the temple is therefore the visible sign that the old covenant age, and with it the whole eschatological drama, was brought to completion.

Dispensationalists accept that 24:2 was fulfilled in AD 70. They argue, however, that Jesus' answer to the further questions about his coming and the end of the age reaches beyond that event, and that a future temple will be rebuilt and desecrated (Daniel 9:27; 2 Thessalonians 2:4; Revelation 11:1–2).

Historic premillennialists read 24:1–2 as a firm prediction of AD 70 that serves as the springboard for the discourse. The near judgment on the temple is a pledge of the far judgment at Christ's return, and Jesus' answer moves between the two.

The temple's destruction marks the end of the shadow and the arrival of the reality: Christ and his people are now the temple (John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:19–22). Amillennialists therefore see no future role for a rebuilt temple, while also seeing AD 70 as a preview of final judgment.

Classic historicists such as Thomas Newton opened their treatment of Matthew 24 by showing from Josephus how exactly the temple prophecy was fulfilled, treating it as one of the clearest proofs of Christ's prophetic authority, before tracing later prophecies through church history.

Jesus turns the disciples' eyes from stones to himself. A religion built around a physical sanctuary, however beautiful, was about to give way to the living temple of Christ's body and the Spirit's dwelling in believers, and the destruction makes that transfer unmistakable.
Titus orders the city razed

Josephus says Titus ordered the whole city and temple demolished except three towers and part of the western wall, kept to show the strength of what Rome had conquered, and that the rest was levelled so thoroughly that visitors would hardly believe it had been inhabited.
The sanctuary burned

Josephus describes a soldier throwing a firebrand into the sanctuary, the fire spreading despite (he says) Titus' orders, and the holy house burning on the same day of the year as Solomon's temple was burned by the Babylonians.
Some stones remained

The retaining walls of the temple platform, including the Western Wall, still stand, so critics ask whether “not one stone” was fulfilled literally. Most interpreters answer that Jesus spoke of the temple buildings the disciples were admiring, which were entirely destroyed, and that the saying is proverbial for complete ruin.
Whether the temple's destruction is the controlling subject of the whole discourse, or only the opening occasion for a prophecy that then reaches to the end of history.
The disciples' questions

On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask privately when “these things” will be, and what will be the sign of Jesus' coming (parousia) and of the end of the age. Mark and Luke ask only about “these things” and their sign.

The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron valley and was associated with the day of the Lord in Zechariah 14:4, where the Lord's feet stand on it. Parousia was used of a royal visit or official arrival as well as of a person's presence; synteleia tou aiōnos (end of the age) is a phrase almost unique to Matthew (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20). Jewish writers commonly divided history into “this age” and “the age to come”.

Because Mark and Luke record only a question about the temple, Matthew's wording shows how the disciples understood that event: the temple's fall would be the coming of the Messiah in judgment and the end of the old covenant age. The answer up to 24:34 addresses this, and Jesus then speaks of the final day in 24:36 onward.

Matthew presents one question with three linked parts, and the answer treats them as a unity. If the temple fell in AD 70, then the parousia and the end of the age happened then too; to separate them is to impose a later theology on the text.

The disciples asked about two or three distinct events, and Jesus' answer distinguishes them. Luke gives the answer about the temple, while Matthew focuses on the sign of the coming and the end of the age, which belong to the future tribulation and return. The disciples' assumption that all would happen together was mistaken, as Jesus' warning “the end is not yet” (24:6) begins to show.

The disciples assumed one event; Jesus did not correct them directly but gave an answer in which near and far are both present. Parousia in 1 Thessalonians 4:15 and 1 Corinthians 15:23 is the future bodily return, and Matthew's use should be read in harmony with that.

The disciples' fused question is answered with a fused answer. Since the temple's fall and the end of the world are theologically linked as judgment and its type, Jesus describes them together, and the reader must discern which features belong to which horizon.

The disciples ask about signs and timing; Jesus answers by warning them against deception and calling them to endurance and watchfulness. The real question beneath theirs is what replaces the temple, and the answer is the Son of Man himself, enthroned and present with his people.
Mark and Luke ask only about the temple
Mark 13:4 and Luke 21:7 frame the question solely around “these things”, the temple's destruction, suggesting that Matthew's added phrases interpret that same event.
Parousia elsewhere means the bodily return

Every other New Testament use of parousia for Christ (1 Corinthians 15:23; 1 Thessalonians 2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23; 2 Thessalonians 2:1, 8; James 5:7–8; 2 Peter 3:4; 1 John 2:28) is commonly read of his personal return, which futurists argue sets the meaning in Matthew 24.
“End of the age” in Matthew

Matthew's other uses (13:39–49, the harvest and separation of the righteous and wicked; 28:20, Christ's presence with the church) tie the phrase to final judgment, which futurists stress; preterists reply that the judgment of 13:40–42 is a harvest of the covenant people and fits the close of the old age.
Whether the disciples asked one question or several, and whether Jesus' answer keeps their parts together or separates them.
Deceivers, wars, famines and earthquakes

Jesus warns that many will come in his name saying “I am the Christ” and deceive many. There will be wars and rumours of wars, nation against nation, famines and earthquakes in various places, but “the end is not yet”; these are “the beginning of birth pains”.

“Birth pains” (ōdines) was a stock image in the prophets and later Jewish writings for the suffering before God's deliverance (Isaiah 13:8; 26:17–19; Jeremiah 22:23; Micah 4:9–10); later rabbis spoke of “the birth pangs of the Messiah”. The years between Jesus' ministry and AD 70 saw Roman wars in Britain, Armenia and Parthia, unrest in Judea and Alexandria, famine under Claudius, and earthquakes in Asia Minor and Italy.

These were all fulfilled before AD 70 and are what Jesus' first hearers would experience: Josephus' impostors, the Claudian famine (Acts 11:28), the earthquakes at Laodicea and Pompeii, and the wars culminating in the civil wars of AD 69. Jesus' point is that such events are not themselves the end, so the disciples must not panic or follow false messiahs.

Full preterists read this section the same way as partial preterists, as signs fulfilled in AD 30–70 before the climactic judgment, and use it to underline that every sign Jesus gave was experienced by his own generation.

Many dispensationalists see these as the general characteristics of the age that will intensify into the first half of the seven-year tribulation, matching the first four seals of Revelation 6. Others treat them as signs of the whole age leading to the tribulation. Either way, Jesus' words describe the period just before his return rather than the 60s.

Such troubles mark the whole interval between the advents and do not by themselves signal the end. Historic premillennialists see them as recurring signs that grow towards a final crisis, and stress that the church must endure them.

These signs characterise the entire age between Christ's comings; they are reminders that the end is coming rather than calendar markers. The first century experienced them, as has every century since.

Historicists accept the first-century fulfilment and add that the pattern continued in the wars and calamities that followed the fall of Rome, which many correlated with the seals and trumpets of Revelation.

The birth-pain image shows that history's convulsions are not meaningless: they are labour leading to new creation (Romans 8:22). The signs are permanent features of a fallen world under God's rule, calling believers to discernment rather than date-setting.
Famine under Claudius

Acts 11:28 says Agabus predicted a great famine over the whole oikoumenē, which took place under Claudius; Josephus describes a severe famine in Judea about AD 46–48, relieved by Queen Helena of Adiabene, and Suetonius mentions repeated crop failures in Claudius' reign.
Earthquakes in various places

Tacitus records that Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 60 and rebuilt without Roman aid, and that Pompeii was largely overthrown by an earthquake in AD 62 (Seneca dates it to 63). Josephus describes a terrifying storm with earthquake over Jerusalem in 68.
Wars and rumours of wars
Tacitus opens his Histories describing the period from 69 as rich in disasters, frightful in battles and torn by civil strife, with four emperors killed by the sword.
Not unique to the first century

Futurists and amillennialists point out that wars, famines and earthquakes have occurred in every century, so their presence before 70 does not show that the discourse was exhausted then; Jesus himself says they are only “the beginning”.
Whether these general signs were meant to be fulfilled within the disciples' lifetime, or to characterise the whole age, or to intensify in a final period.
Persecution, apostasy and the gospel to the whole world

The disciples will be handed over, killed and hated by all nations. Many will fall away and betray one another; false prophets will arise; love will grow cold. The one who endures to the end will be saved. “This gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world (oikoumenē) as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.”

Oikoumenē means “the inhabited world”, usually as Greek and Roman writers knew it; Luke uses it of the Roman empire's census (Luke 2:1) and of the famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Mark has “to all nations” (13:10). Luke's parallel says the persecution will come “before all this” (21:12), that is, before the signs of 21:10–11. The disciples' experience in Acts and Paul's letters matches the list closely: councils, synagogues, governors, kings, betrayal and martyrdom.

Every item was fulfilled before AD 70: the apostles were handed over to councils and governors, James and Stephen were killed, Nero made Christians the objects of hatred, false teachers and apostasy plagued the churches, and by the 60s Paul could say the gospel had reached the whole oikoumenē (Romans 10:18; Colossians 1:6, 23). “The end” is then the end of the age the disciples asked about, the temple's fall.

Postmillennialists, mostly preterist on this section, stress that 24:14 was fulfilled in principle by the apostolic mission to the known world before 70, and that the Great Commission then continues to bring the nations to Christ through history. The end of the old order is the beginning of the gospel's worldwide growth, not the end of its progress.

The worldwide preaching describes the testimony during the future tribulation, which some connect with the 144,000 and the two witnesses or the angel proclaiming the eternal gospel (Revelation 7; 11; 14:6). “The end” is the end of the tribulation and the return of Christ. Paul's hyperbolic statements about the gospel's spread do not exhaust a promise that it will reach “all nations”.

Historic premillennialists such as Ladd see 24:14 as the church's mission throughout the age: the gospel must go to every people before Christ returns. The verse makes missions part of the eschatological programme, and the church will endure persecution until the end.

Many amillennialists hold a double reference: the apostolic mission fulfilled the verse in a first sense before 70, but the larger fulfilment is the gospel reaching all nations before the final end (Matthew 28:19–20; Revelation 7:9). Persecution and apostasy likewise characterise the whole age.
Historicists accepted the apostolic fulfilment and saw the continuing spread of the gospel, including the Reformation and modern missions, as part of the prophesied history leading to the end.

The section describes the church's permanent situation: hated by the world, tested by false teaching and cold love, yet bearing witness to all nations. Endurance, not escape, is the mark of true discipleship in every age.
Paul's universal language before 70

Paul writes that the Romans' faith is proclaimed in all the world (Romans 1:8), that the message has gone out to the ends of the oikoumenē (Romans 10:18), that the gospel is bearing fruit in the whole world (Colossians 1:6) and has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven (Colossians 1:23; compare Romans 16:26).
Christians hated and killed

Tacitus says Nero blamed the fire of Rome on Christians, a class “hated for their abominations”, and had them torn by dogs, crucified and burned as torches. Josephus records the stoning of James the Lord's brother in AD 62.
“All nations” and “the end”

Futurists note that Mark has “all nations” (panta ta ethnē), the phrase of the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19), and that Jesus ties this preaching to “the end” (to telos) rather than to the temple's fall. Many peoples remained unreached in AD 70, and Revelation 14:6 pictures a final universal proclamation.
The meaning of oikoumenē

Oikoumenē often meant the Roman world (Luke 2:1; Acts 11:28; 17:6; 24:5), which supports a first-century fulfilment; but it can also mean the whole inhabited earth (Acts 17:31; Hebrews 2:5), so the word alone does not settle the question.
Whether “the whole world” and “all nations” in 24:14 were reached by the apostolic mission before AD 70, or still await fulfilment before the final end.
The abomination of desolation and the flight from Judea

“When you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those in Judea flee to the mountains.” No one should go back for belongings; it will be hard for pregnant and nursing women; they should pray their flight is not in winter or on a Sabbath. Luke's parallel reads: “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near.”

Daniel speaks of an abomination that makes desolate in 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11. Jews of Jesus' day knew a fulfilment in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up a pagan altar on the altar of burnt offering (1 Maccabees 1:54) and stopped the sacrifices. Roman standards bearing images had already provoked crises under Pilate, and Caligula's attempt to place his statue in the temple in AD 40 was within living memory when the Gospels were written. Mark's grammatically masculine “standing where he ought not” suggests a person or personified power.

Luke 21:20 is the inspired commentary on the parallel: the abomination that brings desolation is the Roman armies surrounding Jerusalem, which entered the holy precincts and, according to Josephus, set up their standards in the temple court and sacrificed to them. Many add the Zealots' profanation of the temple, which Josephus described as a pollution that fulfilled an ancient oracle. The command to flee was obeyed, as Eusebius records, when Jerusalem's Christians escaped to Pella.
Full preterists hold the same view of the abomination as partial preterists and treat it as the decisive sign within the one AD 70 scenario that also includes the coming and the end of the age.

Daniel 9:27 places the abomination in the middle of the seventieth week, after the Messiah is cut off, and Daniel 12:11 links it to the time of the end and the resurrection (12:1–2). Since Paul (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4) and John (Revelation 13:14–15) also describe a future desecration by a personal Antichrist, Matthew 24:15 must refer to a future rebuilt temple. Luke 21:20–24 describes AD 70, which was a related but distinct event.

Historic premillennialists such as Ladd see AD 70 as a real fulfilment that also foreshadows a final Antichrist figure. The prophecy has a near and a far horizon, and the Jerusalem setting of the near fulfilment does not exhaust it.

The Roman desecration in AD 70 fulfilled the prophecy, and Luke makes this plain. Some amillennialists also see it as a type of the final apostasy and man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2), which will arise within the professing church rather than in a rebuilt temple.

Classic historicists generally saw AD 70 as the fulfilment of 24:15, often citing the Roman standards; the later desecration of the church by the papacy, sitting in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4), was a separate prophecy fulfilled through the centuries.

The abomination is anything set up in the holy place in place of God, from the idolatry of a temple religion that rejected its Messiah to any substitute for Christ in the heart. The call to flee is a call to leave a system doomed to destruction and find refuge in him.
Luke: Jerusalem surrounded by armies
Luke, in the same position in the discourse and with the same command to flee to the mountains, explains the sign as Jerusalem surrounded by armies and its desolation drawing near.
Standards in the temple court
After the temple was burned, the Romans brought their standards into the temple court, set them opposite the eastern gate, offered sacrifices to them and acclaimed Titus as imperator.
The flight to Pella

Eusebius says the Jerusalem church, commanded by an oracle given to approved men before the war, left the city and lived in Pella in Perea. Epiphanius repeats the tradition. Some scholars (for example S. G. F. Brandon) doubted it, but others (Craig Koester) defend its essential historicity.
Daniel's sequence and Paul's man of lawlessness

Daniel 12:11 ties the abomination to the time of the end and the resurrection that follows (12:1–2), and 2 Thessalonians 2:3–8 speaks of a lawless one taking his seat in the temple of God and being destroyed by Christ's coming. Futurists argue that no AD 70 figure matches this person or event.
Whether Luke 21:20 interprets Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14 (a single AD 70 event), or Luke describes AD 70 while Matthew and Mark describe a future Antichrist in a rebuilt temple.
Great tribulation, unequalled

“There will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be.” If those days had not been cut short, no flesh would be saved, but for the sake of the elect they will be shortened. Luke speaks of great distress on the land and wrath against this people, who will fall by the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

The wording echoes Daniel 12:1 (“a time of trouble such as never has been”) and similar hyperbolic formulas in Exodus 11:6, Joel 2:2 and Ezekiel 5:9. During the siege Jerusalem was crowded with Passover pilgrims, three factions fought one another, and famine killed vast numbers. The siege lasted about five months, from Passover to late summer of AD 70.

The siege of Jerusalem was the great tribulation. Josephus, who had no Christian motive, says the miseries of all peoples since the world began were small compared to those of the Jews. The formula “such as never has been” is covenantal hyperbole used in Exodus 11:6 and Ezekiel 5:9 of events that were later surpassed in scale; what made AD 70 unique was its covenantal significance as the climax of judgment on the old covenant people (Matthew 23:35–36). The days were shortened because Titus pressed the siege quickly.

As with partial preterism, the tribulation is AD 66–70; full preterists add that the “elect” for whose sake the days were shortened are the first-century church, whose deliverance was its redemption at the parousia.

The language is absolute: never before and never again. AD 70, however terrible, was surpassed in scale by later catastrophes, including the Holocaust, and Luke 21:24 shows that Jerusalem's suffering continued afterward. This must be the future great tribulation, the second half of Daniel's seventieth week (Daniel 12:1; Revelation 7:14), which ends with Christ's return “immediately after” (24:29) and threatens all flesh.

Futurists in general argue that “no flesh would be saved” describes a threat to all humanity, matching Revelation's worldwide judgments, which a regional siege does not fully meet. The appeal to Daniel 12:1, which is followed by the resurrection, also points to the end.

The tribulation began with AD 70 but the final great tribulation lies ahead, and the church will pass through it before Christ's return. The elect for whose sake the days are shortened are believers, the church, not a separate Jewish group.

The great tribulation is the suffering of God's people through the whole age, of which AD 70 was an intense early expression, with a final intensification before Christ returns (Revelation 7:14 speaks of those coming out of the great tribulation).

Adventist historicists apply the great tribulation of 24:21 to the long persecution of faithful Christians by papal Rome during the 1260 years, which they date AD 538–1798, and see the shortening of those days in the decline of persecution before the end of that period.
Josephus: the greatest of all calamities

In the preface to his history Josephus says the misfortunes of all men from the beginning of the world were not so considerable as those of the Jews, and later that no other city ever suffered such miseries.
Numbers killed and captured
Josephus gives 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 captives; Tacitus says 600,000 were besieged. Modern historians think Josephus' figures are inflated but agree the death toll was enormous.
“Never will be” and the Holocaust

Futurists argue that later events, such as the Holocaust, in which about six million Jews were killed, exceeded AD 70 in scale, so the absolute language of 24:21 points to a still-future time. Preterists reply that the uniqueness lies in covenant significance, not body count.
Luke 21:24 extends past AD 70

Luke says the people will be led captive among the nations and Jerusalem trampled until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled, an open-ended period after the siege. Futurists argue that this places Jesus' coming in Luke 21:25–28 after a long interval.
Whether the superlative language of 24:21 is prophetic hyperbole fulfilled in AD 70, or describes a still-future tribulation that will exceed anything in history.
False christs, lightning and the eagles

If anyone says “Here is the Christ” or “There he is”, do not believe it: false christs and false prophets will perform great signs to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. If they say he is in the wilderness or in the inner rooms, do not go. The coming of the Son of Man will be like lightning from east to west. “Wherever the corpse is, there the eagles (or vultures) will gather.”

Josephus' impostors led crowds into the wilderness promising signs of deliverance, and during the siege a prophet summoned people into the temple to receive such signs. The Greek aetos means eagle and was used loosely for large carrion birds; the aquila, the eagle standard of each Roman legion, was the army's sacred emblem. Lightning from the east to the west recalls the visibility of God's appearing in judgment (Zechariah 9:14).

The false prophets with signs in the wilderness are the impostors Josephus describes in the years before and during the war. The lightning image says Christ's coming in judgment would not be a secret local appearance but would sweep across the land from east to west, as the Roman armies did when they swept through Galilee and Judea to Jerusalem. The eagles gathering over the corpse are the Roman legions, with their eagle standards, gathering around the dead body of apostate Jerusalem.
The coming like lightning is the AD 70 parousia, a manifestation of Christ in judgment that was public and unmistakable to those who had eyes to see, rather than a physical appearance on the earth.

During the future tribulation many will claim to be the Messiah, and the false prophet of Revelation 13:13–14 will work great signs. Christ's actual return will be sudden, visible and universal like lightning across the sky, so no one needs to be told where he is. The carcass and birds point to the battle of Armageddon and the birds feasting on the slain (Revelation 19:17–21).

The warning against secret comings shows that Christ's return will be public and visible to all, which historic premillennialists contrast with a secret pretribulational rapture. The bird image proverbially means that judgment falls wherever corruption is found.

The verses distinguish the visible, unmistakable final coming from all false claims to messianic presence in this age. The proverb of the corpse and the vultures means judgment will come wherever spiritual death is found, whether in AD 70 or at the end.

False christs appear in every age, offering hidden or spectacular salvation. The true Christ needs no advertising: his coming will be as obvious as lightning. The proverb teaches that judgment always finds what is dead.

The church must not look for Christ in the wilderness of religious striving or in hidden inner rooms of special knowledge. He is revealed openly, like light filling the sky, and the dead carcass of a religion without him attracts only scavengers.
Impostors leading crowds to the wilderness
Josephus describes deceivers who, under pretence of divine inspiration, led people into the wilderness promising signs of freedom, and the Egyptian who led a crowd to the Mount of Olives.
A false prophet in the temple

On the day the temple burned, about six thousand people had gone up to a portico because a false prophet had proclaimed that God commanded them to go there to receive the signs of their deliverance; all perished.
Eagles or vultures?

Preterists connect aetoi with the Roman eagle standards; many commentators reply that the saying is a proverb about carrion birds (Job 39:27–30; Luke 17:37), so the Roman link is possible but not certain.
A universal, visible coming
Futurists argue that lightning “from east to west” describes a coming visible across the sky to all, matching Revelation 1:7 (“every eye will see him”) and Acts 1:11, not a military campaign.
Whether the lightning-like coming is a visible bodily return or the sudden sweep of Christ's judgment through Rome's armies, and whether the eagles are the legions or a proverb.
Immediately after: sun, moon and stars

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.” Luke adds distress of nations, perplexity at the roaring of the sea, and people fainting with fear.

The verse weaves together Isaiah 13:10 (the fall of Babylon) and Isaiah 34:4 (judgment on Edom and the nations), with echoes of Ezekiel 32:7 (Egypt) and Joel 2:10, 31. In the ancient world the heavenly bodies were associated with rulers and gods, and the falling of stars could symbolise the fall of powers. Josephus and Tacitus both report portents in the sky before and during the war.

Jesus uses the prophets' standard language for the fall of a nation. As Isaiah described Babylon's fall as the darkening of sun and stars, so Jesus describes the collapse of Jerusalem's world, its rulers and its temple-centred order, “immediately after” the tribulation of the siege. Ancient Jewish hearers would have recognised the idiom and not expected an astronomical event.
